about: The Barrow-Kin's king-barrow: a deep site generated from what it was for. They laid their first king under a mound on the bounds of their land, in a stone grave below the halls where his people were laid round him, and sealed the way down to him with a seal-stone. Levels follow the dead down: the passage-grave under the mound, the halls of the dead, the king's grave. A portal stone on a counterweight closes the stair behind the passage-grave; the king's door is sealed and the makers' warning cut round it; grave-robbers have dug their own way to the king's treasury; a light-box over the door lets in a thread of daylight and is a second way out. Roles give each room its names and its scene. Written by hand.

plan.seen: a great long mound with a door of stone

names: a gap where the bones have fallen
the stair behind the portal stone

scenes: A forecourt of standing stones faces the sunrise, curving in to the mound's high end. Between the two tallest is the door, a low black square under a lintel of one stone.
A passage of upright slabs runs into the mound, roofed with stones laid across, so low you go bent. The slabs are cut with spirals and with lines that might be roads.

The passage opens into a chamber shaped like a cross, its roof rising in stones laid each a little further in than the one below until one stone closes it. Basins of stone stand in the arms, with ash in them.
A recess off the chamber, with a basin of stone in it and the burned bones of the first-laid heaped in the basin, a bead or two among them.
A recess where the slabs are carved closer than anywhere else, all with the same sign: an eye, or a sun, or a door.

finds.cue: a bead or two among them
finds.found: Among the burned bones in the basin, a string of amber beads, the cord gone to nothing and the beads still in their order.

scenes: A slot in the stones over the door, a box of slabs open to the sky at one end: on one morning of the year the sun comes through it and down the whole length of the passage. It is wide enough for a body to squeeze through.
Under the overhang of the forecourt someone has camped: a hearth of three stones, a bundle of picks, a sack with the bottom cut out.

The chamber's far arm ends in a single stone taller than the rest, smooth, uncarved; behind it, where it does not quite meet the wall, a draught comes up from below. A portal stone hangs in a slot in the rock beside it.
The stair comes down into a low hall cut in the chalk under the mound, white walls gone grey with the smoke of lamps long out. Niches run away along both walls in rows.
A long hall of niches, every niche with its dead in it, laid on their sides with their knees drawn up as if asleep, a pot by each head. The floor is swept, as if someone had swept it.
A hall with a hearth and benches cut in the chalk, where the living sat with the dead the night before a burial. Bone flutes hang on pegs along the wall, a whole row of them, long silent.
Bones stacked in walls: skulls in rows between courses of long bones, built up to the roof like masonry. In one place the wall has fallen, and someone has dug through behind it.
A gallery runs on under the halls, its walls painted with people walking all one way, toward the end of it, each carrying something: a pot, a child, a flute, a light.
A room of stone tables and stone basins, where the dead were made ready. Jars stand in niches, sealed with clay and marked, and the air still smells faintly of resin.
A shaft drops away in the floor, ringed with a low kerb worn smooth by hands. Far down, something white catches your light: what was thrown in.
The gallery ends at a door: two posts and a lintel of single stones, carved closer than anything else in the halls, round a black opening as tall as a man.
Beyond the door the chalk gives way to old dark rock. A small chamber, empty but for a stone bench and the marks of the many who have knelt before it.
A low room of stone shelves, most of them bare now. On the floor, a rotted sack, a pick, and a man's bones lie where the robbers' tunnel comes through the wall.

The grave of the first king is a hall, not a grave: a ring of standing stones under the rock, and in the middle of the ring a bier of stone, with a cloak gone to dust on it in the shape of whoever lay there.
Behind the ring a pit goes down into the rock, its sides smooth, and a smell comes up out of it like turned earth. Whatever lies at the bottom of it is not the king, or is not only the king.

words.Warns: The king sits up on his bier, slowly, the way a man sits up who has been called, and turns his face toward you. There is no face, only the crown.
words.Flinches: The light of day comes into the king's hall with you, and the king puts up an arm against it as the living do, and goes back from it, step by step, into the deep grave behind the ring.

bane.seen: In one niche, behind the sealed jars, stands a jar of thick old glass stoppered with clay, and it is full of light: not lamplight, but daylight.
bane.cut: HE CANNOT ABIDE THE DAY. THE EMBALMERS KEPT THE DAY IN A JAR.
bane.fact: What sleeps in the king's grave cannot abide the light of day; the embalmers of the Barrow-Kin kept day in a jar against it.

objective.item: the crown of the first king
objective.text: The Barrow-Kin buried their first king with the crown they made him out of the first gold of their land, and laid his people round him to keep him. Whoever brings the crown out from under the mound has the bounds' own crown.
objective.goal: Bring the crown of the first king out from under {name}.
objective.raised: In the daylight the crown of the first king, out from under {name} at last, is only a crown, a ring of soft gold, very old, and the day is the same day it was.

rumours: 'The king-barrow at {name}? The old folk's first king is under it, they say, with his crown on, and all his people round him. Robbers go in every few years. Some come out.'
'There was a man went into {name} after the king's gold and came out with a pocket of amber and his hair gone white. Grave-goods, gold, jet, amber: I buy them and I do not ask whose they were.'

land.blight: No bird sits on the mound. The grass on it grows long and pale and nothing grazes it, though the sheep crop the field round it to the stones.

signs.rites: The dead in this mound do not lie still. The grass over the chambers is pressed flat in the mornings as though something had lain on it all night, and got up again before the sun.
signs.woodcraft: Hares lie out on every field round here but this one, and the owls hunt the mound and nothing else. Whatever comes up out of it by night, the voles keep well away from.

land.healed: A blackbird is singing on the mound, and the sheep have come up onto it to graze.

trade.topic: what is buried in the king-barrow
trade.says: weighs a bead of amber on a fingertip. 'Bring me what the old folk buried and I will pay what it is worth.'

hook.home: 'Out from under {name}?' {keeper} puts down the jug and looks a long while at the crown, and does not touch it. 'My grandmother said the king would keep it till the mound fell in. Tonight you eat and sleep on the house, and I will be telling this in the taproom for a year.'

camp.later: The same party camped here too, further in: the ring of stones again, a smaller fire, and less left beside it than outside, a blanket and an empty water-skin, as if they were travelling lighter by now.
camp.scene: Someone camped here, and not so long ago: a ring of stones round dead ashes, a bedroll gone stiff with damp, a pack with its straps cut. They did not come back for any of it.
journal: A notebook, swollen with damp. 'The portal stone is down and its weight is jammed in the slot. A bar under the weight would free it, Brann says. The light comes in through a box over the door at sunrise; we got in that way.'

A notebook, the last pages written small. 'The king's door is sealed with a stone and there are words round it nobody can read. The robbers have dug round it through the ossuary, and they did not come back. In the embalmers' room there is a jar that is warm to the touch.'
A notebook with one line in it, written by someone lying down: 'he is not asleep'.

outside: The mound lies long on the land, grassed over, higher at its east end. At the high end a forecourt of standing stones curves in to the door, and on the lintel, cut in the old script: {oldup}.

negligible.name: a string of amber beads
negligible.text: Amber beads on a cord gone to nothing, warm-coloured even in the dark.

negligible.name: a jet button
negligible.text: A button of black jet, polished, with a hole drilled through it on the slant.

negligible.name: a bone flute
negligible.text: A flute made from the leg-bone of a crane, with four holes; the Barrow-Kin spoke with their dead through flutes like it.

minor.name: a bronze mirror
minor.text: A disc of bronze, its back cast with spirals, its face gone green: you can still see yourself in it, darkly.

minor.name: a silver arm-ring
minor.text: A ring of twisted silver made to be worn above the elbow.

minor.name: a gold cloak-pin
minor.text: A pin of gold with a head like a sun, for a cloak that rotted round it.

major.name: a gold torc
major.text: A torc of twisted gold, heavy, its ends cast as two heads looking at each other.

major.name: a jet necklace
major.text: A necklace of jet plates and beads, strung in the order they were found, black and bright.

major.name: a bronze shield-boss
major.text: The bronze boss of a shield long gone, cast with a face.

grand.name: a gold lunula
grand.text: A crescent of beaten gold, thin as a leaf, made to lie on a breast: a queen's, or a priest's.

grand.name: a gold cup
grand.text: A cup beaten out of a single piece of gold, corrugated like a shell, made for one drink.

winch.seized: The portal stone stands down across the stair behind the back-stone, and its counterweight hangs jammed in its slot, wedged with fallen stone.
winch.turning: The counterweight runs free in its slot, and the portal stone can be raised off the stair and let down again.
winch.shut: A portal stone stands down across the stair, as heavy as a house-wall, and its counterweight will not move.
winch.climb: the gap over the portal stone

seal.thing: the seal-stone across the king's door
seal.noun: the sealed door of the king-barrow
seal.standing: A seal-stone as tall as a man closes the king's door, its edges packed with clay and the clay marked with handprints.
seal.broken: The seal-stone lies cracked across the threshold, and the king's door stands open.
seal.rebuild: Set the seal-stone back across the king's door
seal.words: the words cut round the king's door
seal.unread: Words are cut all round the king's door, in the old script, deep and close. Someone who reads the old script could say what they mean.
seal.readLabel: Read what is cut round the king's door
seal.read: {oldup}. HERE THE KING KEEPS THE BOUNDS. LET HIM KEEP THEM. {FATE}
seal.told: Read aloud, the old words say plainly enough who is behind the door, and what he cannot abide.

vent.found: Where the light and the air come from: the light-box over the door, a slot of stones a body could squeeze through, out to the top of the mound.
vent.sign: A thread of grey daylight lies along the floor of the passage, coming from somewhere above the door.
vent.night: A breath of night air comes along the floor of the passage, from somewhere above the door, and it smells of grass.
vent.rungs: the climb out over the lintel

warlords.scene: Someone after the Barrow-Kin made a fort of the forecourt: a bank of earth thrown up across it, with a palisade's post-holes along the top, and a ditch the grass has half filled.

document.name: the words cut on the passage stone
document.shut: On one slab of the passage someone has cut words in the kingdom's letters, not the old script, over the spirals.
document.label: Read the words on the passage stone
document.text: HELD FOR THE LORD OF {kingdomup}. WHOEVER GOES DOWN GOES DOWN BY HIS LEAVE.

abbots.scene: The brothers who came after the Barrow-Kin hung a bell in the mourners' hall and cut their sign over the hearth, and said their own prayers for the old dead.

document.name: the brothers' tablet
document.shut: A slate tablet hangs on a peg among the bone flutes, written over in a careful hand.
document.label: Read the brothers' tablet
document.text: The brothers of {kingdom} prayed here for the dead of the old folk, and sealed the king's door a second time with a blessing. Let no one break it, and let the old king keep his bounds.

valuable.name: a brothers' hand-bell
valuable.text: A hand-bell of bronze with the brothers' sign cast on it, rung for the dead.

princes.scene: The merchant-princes after the Barrow-Kin sent men down for the king's gold: their tally of what they took is scratched on the wall, and stops after the third line.

document.name: a scratched tally
document.shut: Lines are scratched in the wall by the robbers' tunnel, in the kingdom's letters.
document.label: Read the scratched tally
document.text: For the {kingdom} company: four torcs, a cup, eleven pins of gold. The men will not go past the ring. Given up.

plague.scene: When the plague came, the town laid its own dead in the old king's recesses, wrapped in sacking, and limed them, and went away.

winter.scene: In the long winter people lived in the passage-grave, where the cold could not get in: there are hearths in the arms of the chamber, and the basins have been used to cook in.

heirs.scene: In the war of the heirs someone climbed down into the well of offerings with something to hide: there are new knots in an old rope tied to the kerb.

hidden.found: At the bottom of the well, among the offerings, a strongbox someone lowered in the war of the heirs.

valuable.name: an heir's strongbox
valuable.text: An iron box with a broken seal, full of the coin of a kingdom that no longer exists.

raiders.scene: Raiders from over the sea dug into the forecourt one summer looking for gold, and gave up: there is a trench half across it, and a broken spade in the bottom.
